extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political history and constitutional design
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and assessing normative lessons and constitutional principles drawn from the history of ancient Greek democracies (Athens, Sparta, Thebes, etc.) as presented in a historical/political treatise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple democracy is impracticable; people cannot manage the executive
rubrics_metrics.description: "the people in a body cannot manage the executive power, and therefore that a simple democracy is impracticable"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues that popular bodies lack capacity to administer executive functions; a purely popular government is unstable and prone to abuses. This is presented as a general normative lesson from Athens' experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative power must be tempered with two other branches (mixed constitution)
rubrics_metrics.description: "their share of the legislative power must be always tempered with two others, in order to enable them to preserve their share, as well as to correct its rapid tendency to abuse."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mixed constitution (legislature balanced by two other powers) is recommended to preserve popular authority while preventing its excesses. Solon's attempt at a 'double balance' is discussed and judged inferior to a true tripartite balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: A single assembly (single-branch government) produces anarchy and profligacy
rubrics_metrics.description: "the government of a single assembly of archons chosen by the people, was found intolerable... by introducing anarchy, and such a general profligacy of manners"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Governments centered in one popular assembly are criticized as leading to faction, massacres, proscriptions, banishment, and the death of the best citizens (Thucydides cited). The passage treats single-assembly polities as constitutionally defective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tripartite separation of powers is the effective safeguard
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples and praise for a legislature divided into three branches so "that no law can be passed in a passion, nor inconsistent with the constitution."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author contrasts Solon's 'double balance' with systems (e.g., modern English/US arrangements) where executive, legislative, and judiciary are distinct; such separation prevents laws passed in passion and guards against sudden abuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive must be excluded from legislative assemblies; judiciary must be independent
rubrics_metrics.description: "The executive is excluded from the two legislative assemblies; and the judiciary power is independent, as well as separate from all."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific separation rules: executives should not sit in legislative bodies; judicial independence and institutional separation are essential parts of a durable constitution (offered as features of the U.S. federal model).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ostracism and checks that merely banish the popular or great men are injudicious
rubrics_metrics.description: "The ostracism ... only banished their best men. History nowhere furnishes so frank a confession of the people themselves, of their own infirmities... We know our heads will be turned... we shall always make them kings."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measures that simply prevent prominent citizens from serving (or exile them) can eliminate effective leaders and are an unreliable and damaging check on ambition; the author calls ostracism a melancholy, injudicious device.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional design shapes civic character and elite behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: "Such a constitution of government, and the education of youth which follows necessarily from it, always produces such characters as Cleon and Alcibiades... mixtures of good qualities enough to acquire the confidence of a party, and bad ones enough to lead them to destruction."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The regime type conditions the formation of political leaders; democracies without proper balance produce demagogues and volatile elites. This is offered as an evaluative criterion when judging systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale and federal structure mitigate the dangers of direct democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: "Planted as they are over large dominions, they cannot meet in one assembly, and therefore are not exposed to those tumultuous commotions ... they have all elections ... so prudently guarded, that there is scarce a possibility of intrigue."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Larger, federal polities (like the United States) are defended as less prone to the direct-democracy pathologies of classical Athens because of scale, representative institutions, and guarded electoral rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility/property requirements influence openness and electoral competition
rubrics_metrics.description: "The property required in a representative, senator, or even governor, is so small, that multitudes have equal pretensions to be chosen."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Low barriers to eligibility (small property requirements) broaden access to office and prevent elections from being confined to nobility or great wealth; eligibility rules are therefore a substantive design criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fragmentation into many independent small states weakens collective security and invites manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Account of Antalcidas' treaty: declaring small cities 'totally independent of each other' "twisted to atoms... every democratical city and confederacy" leading to weakened confederacies and enabling external domination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Breaking federations or leagues into many independent polities undermines mutual support and makes them vulnerable to foreign interference and subjugation. Unity or stronger confederal ties are thus treated as necessary for resilience.

rubrics_metrics.name: External powers exploit internal factionalism by backing aristocratic (or other) factions
rubrics_metrics.description: Sparta's policy: "supporting the aristocratical factions in all of them, fomenting animosities among the people against each other... Complaints... were referred to the Spartan senate... which always decided in their own favour."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A constitutional system must guard against foreign intervention that leverages internal divisions; external patronage of factions is a predictable threat and a criterion to evaluate institutional robustness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of an effective balancing power (e.g., no king) leads to perpetual factionary violence
rubrics_metrics.description: "No man, no party, ever thought of introducing an effectual balance, by creating a king, with an equal power, to balance the other two. The Romans began to think of this expedient, but it was reserved for England to be the first to reduce it to practice."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author suggests that creating a distinct, balancing executive (such as a monarch) can serve as an effective check on factional strife — a historical lesson for constitutional design to consider additional centers of authority.
